subject: physics_2
question_text: What are the nuclear forces? Write their properties.

verification.note: The 1+1+1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. For this Physics-II paper the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers. Hand-checked: the nuclear force range is about 10⁻¹⁵ m; the relative strengths F_N : F_e : F_G ≈ 10³⁸ : 10³⁶ : 1 are the book's figures and match the standard ratios (strong : electromagnetic : gravitational ≈ 1 : 10⁻² : 10⁻³⁸). The book calls the force "non-central"; that is the tensor part of the force, so this card says the force has a non-central part rather than that it never acts along the line joining the nucleons.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: What nuclear forces are
steps.mark_note: The force that holds nucleons together
lines: Nuclear forces are the strong attractive forces
that act between the nucleons — proton and
proton, proton and neutron, neutron and
neutron — and hold the nucleus together.
steps.margin_note: First mark. Name the three nucleon pairs and the job the force does.
steps.why: The protons in a nucleus repel each other electrically, so a stronger attractive force must be present or no nucleus with two or more protons could exist.
common_mistakes: Calling the nuclear force an electric force. It is a separate, much stronger force.
Saying it acts between electrons and the nucleus.

recall.must_convey: That nuclear forces are the strong attractive forces between nucleons that hold the nucleus together.

steps.memory_tip: Without it the protons would push the nucleus apart at once.

steps.label: Attractive and charge independent
steps.mark_note: Same for p-p, p-n and n-n
lines: 1. They are attractive.
2. They are charge independent: the force is
the same between p-p, p-n and n-n pairs.
3. They are spin dependent: stronger when the
two nucleon spins point the same way.
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Charge independence is the property most often left out.
steps.why: Charge independence is measured, not assumed: the binding of mirror nuclei with protons and neutrons exchanged is the same once the electric repulsion is subtracted.
common_mistakes: Saying the p-p force is weaker. The NUCLEAR force is the same; the electric repulsion is extra.

recall.must_convey: That nuclear forces are attractive, charge independent (same for proton-proton, proton-neutron and neutron-neutron) and spin dependent.
accept: same between p p, p n and n n
reject: range is ten to the power minus fifteen metre

steps.memory_tip: The nuclear force does not look at charge, only at spin and distance.

steps.label: Short range and saturated
steps.mark_note: Range about 10⁻¹⁵ m; saturated; non-central part
lines: 4. They are short range forces, acting only up
to about 10⁻¹⁵ m.
5. They are saturated: one nucleon is bound
only to its nearest neighbours.
6. They have a non-central part, so the force
is not directed only along the line joining
the two nucleons.
steps.margin_note: Third mark. The range figure 10⁻¹⁵ m carries this one.
steps.why: Saturation is why the binding energy per nucleon is almost constant above A ≈ 20: adding a nucleon adds a fixed number of bonds, not a bond to every other nucleon.
common_mistakes: Writing the range as 10⁻¹⁰ m. That is the size of an atom, not of a nucleus.
Saying the force is long range like gravitation.

recall.must_convey: That nuclear forces are short range, acting up to about 10⁻¹⁵ m, are saturated, and have a non-central part.
accept: ten to the power minus fifteen metre

steps.memory_tip: Short range and saturated: a nucleon feels only the neighbours touching it.

steps.label: Exchange forces; strongest
lines: 7. They are exchange forces: the force between
two nucleons arises from the exchange of
π-mesons.
8. They are the strongest forces in nature.
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. The π-meson exchange and the strength ratio.
steps.why: The exchanged particle has mass, and a heavier exchanged particle gives a shorter range — which is how the pion mass and the 10⁻¹⁵ m range are connected.
common_mistakes: Naming photons instead of π-mesons. Photon exchange gives the electric force.
Getting the ratio the wrong way round. The nuclear force is the largest of the three.

recall.must_convey: That nuclear forces are exchange forces due to pi-mesons and are the strongest forces in nature, with the ratio to electric and gravitational forces about 10³⁸ : 10³⁶ : 1.
accept: ten power thirty eight to ten power thirty six to one

steps.memory_tip: Pass a pion between two nucleons and you have the strongest force there is.

insider_note: The examiner marks named properties, not sentences. Four marks means four groups: what it is, charge independence, range, and the exchange picture with the strength ratio.
